title: Choosing a Ruby Code Editor
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of choosing a ruby code editor in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply choosing a ruby code editor in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to terminal integration and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn Choosing a Ruby Code Editor through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding choosing a ruby code editor helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Choosing a Ruby Code Editor helps you reason about syntax highlighting and formatting. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Syntax highlighting and formatting. Then connect it to Ruby language server support. The remaining syllabus points—Navigation, completion, and diagnostics, Terminal integration—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports choosing a ruby code editor. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for choosing a ruby code editor using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Terminal integration), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain choosing a ruby code editor, identify its place in installation and development environment, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
